WITH customer_order_counts AS (
  SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.gender,
    COUNT(o.order_id) as order_count
  FROM Customers c
  LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.gender IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.gender
),
gender_totals AS (
  SELECT 
    gender,
    SUM(order_count) as gender_total_orders
  FROM customer_order_counts
  GROUP BY gender
),
customer_shares AS (
  SELECT 
    coc.customer_id,
    coc.gender,
    coc.order_count,
    CASE 
      WHEN gt.gender_total_orders = 0 THEN NULL
      ELSE coc.order_count * 1.0 / gt.gender_total_orders
    END as share
  FROM customer_order_counts coc
  JOIN gender_totals gt ON coc.gender = gt.gender
),
average_share_calc AS (
  SELECT 
    AVG(share) as avg_share
  FROM customer_shares
)
SELECT 
  cs.customer_id,
  cs.gender,
  cs.order_count,
  cs.share,
  cs.share - asc.avg_share as gap
FROM customer_shares cs
CROSS JOIN average_share_calc asc
ORDER BY gap DESC NULLS LAST
LIMIT 10

assumptions.assumption: Customers with zero orders are included in the analysis. A customer with zero orders in a gender where all customers have zero orders will have a NULL share and NULL gap.
Average share is computed as the arithmetic mean of all individual customer shares (not, e.g., median or weighted by gender).

alternatives.interpretation: Only customers with at least one order are included in the share calculation.
alternatives.sql: Add `HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 0` to the first CTE (customer_order_counts).

alternatives.interpretation: Show only customers whose share exceeds the average (gap > 0), limited to top 10 by gap.
alternatives.sql: Add `WHERE cs.share > asc.avg_share` before the ORDER BY clause in the final SELECT.
